extracted.intended_audience: educational policymakers, program officers, researchers, and administrators involved in vocational/technical education and grant-funded program design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing, evaluating, and funding vocational and technical education experiments and demonstrations that can be applied across secondary and post-secondary systems. Covers curriculum design, teacher preparation, research and evaluation, cooperative work-study, and grant eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of vocational and general education
rubrics_metrics.description: "Vocational education is an integral part of education, particularly at all levels of secondary and post-secondary education, and that improvement of vocational and technical education is the responsibility of all educators, academic and general as well as vocational."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs should eliminate separate, parallel vocational systems; offer vocational and technical subjects as electives alongside academic subjects; allow vocational students access to academic coursework to keep postsecondary options open; and provide college-bound students exposure to vocational training as part of liberal education. Example: Newton Public Schools' effort to end traditional separation and give equal status to vocational and academic studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant eligibility restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Support is not normally given for purely local needs, the routine operating costs of institutions, or building projects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundation grants should target experiments, demonstrations, and activities with potential broader application rather than funding ongoing local operating budgets or capital projects. Preference is for programs with replicable models or research value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for system-wide application / scalability
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects should "contain elements that can strengthen most educational programs" and have potential if "applied in a coordinated, systematic way through the entire educational sequence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and design projects with clear elements that can be scaled or adapted across grades and institutions (elementary through post-secondary), supporting system-wide change rather than isolated pilots. Include plans for dissemination, teacher training, and testing in diverse settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum relevance, transferability, and academic-vocational integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Curricula should focus on transferable work skills and relate academic subject-matter content to shop or laboratory work so vocational content is refocused toward more generally useful skills and concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula that replace narrow occupation-specific training with broader, transferable competencies (e.g., problem-solving, technical literacy). Use coordinated approaches (dovetail technical and academic subjects), team teaching, integrated laboratory/shop experiences, and programmed instruction. Examples: the Richmond Plan (coordinated five-course sequence); Stout State's conceptual industrial-arts curriculum; Western Washington's graphic arts curriculum spanning secondary to community college.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive admissions and student selection by aptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Past academic performance is not a criterion for participation; program enrollment may be based on interest and aptitude (e.g., mechanical aptitude) rather than prior grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit students who might be unmotivated by college-prep courses or at risk of dropping out; use aptitude or interest indicators and provide pathways that keep open options for further education and career mobility. Example: Richmond Plan accepts students with wide-ranging intelligence, including some who were poor students or potential dropouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay tracking and preserve student options
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid forcing youngsters to decide on a vocational track by the ninth grade, since at that age they may not have sufficient opportunity to determine their real interests and aptitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exploratory courses in earlier grades (middle/junior high), personal inventories of interests/abilities, and opportunities to test vocational options before commitment. Ensure vocational programs do not foreclose college access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher preparation combining academic and industry experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation is needed to determine the best means of training thousands of vocational-education teachers for secondary schools, technical institutions, and community colleges; teacher preparation programs should combine generalized and specialized approaches and include internships and industrial experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include interdepartmental studies, summer workshops, supervised internships in schools, paid industry summer sessions, faculty exchanges with industry, and recruitment of experienced industry specialists into accelerated training (e.g., St. Louis Junior College program, Central Michigan, Southern Illinois collaboration). Provide practical industrial experience and supervised teaching practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research, clearinghouse, and topics for study
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is needed on relevance of vocational programs to technological needs and to identify general and transferable work skills; establish clearinghouses of information and research centers to report curricular materials and research findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fund studies analyzing employment histories, transferable skills across occupations, occupational trends, relation of job needs to training, demands on aptitudes/skills/knowledge, problems of disadvantaged groups, counseling and work-study programs, instructional materials, teacher training, and on-the-job training. Support publication and conferences for dissemination (examples: A.I.R., Univ. of Wisconsin center).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and assessment methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use rigorous comparative testing (e.g., experimental groups and control groups), longitudinal follow-up of job placement and job success, and continuous assessment of student progress (test scores, rate of learning, skills acquired).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluations with controls and multiple experimental conditions, track participants over time to measure placement and career outcomes, and implement continuous feedback loops to refine curricula and guidance (example: Oklahoma City dropout study with multiple groups; New York Institute's computerized continuous assessment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cooperative work‑study and credit-for-work arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperative work-study education enables students to alternate periods of regular academic studies with off-campus employment related to their field, and sometimes enables low-income students to finance education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement alternating study/work terms, industry partnerships for supervised on-the-job training, credit for daytime employment (for evening students), employer-subsidized study terms, and programs designed to extend opportunities to disadvantaged groups. Provide coordinator training and use clearinghouses to support new programs (examples: Northeastern, National Commission for Cooperative Education, Bloomfield, Golden Gate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry advisory and placement partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Labor and management representatives serve on advisory boards and help place students; numerous industrial advisory committees exist but their actual effectiveness and composition require study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage employers in curriculum advice, placement assistance, and program planning; evaluate advisory committee effectiveness and composition; involve industry in internships and in updating curricula to match technological change (example: advisory boards for hotel/restaurant programs; Upjohn Institute study recommendation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of technology for individualized guidance and program management
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing the feasibility of using computers in guidance and evaluation to assist in developing individually tailored programs and to keep guidance/evaluation staff requirements within economically feasible bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement computerized information centers for profiling students, predicting performance, designing individualized curricula, feeding continuous assessment data back to staff, and enabling redirection of students to suitable programs. Combine computerized tools with face-to-face counseling as appropriate (example: New York Institute of Technology experiment).
